title: Faith, Sweat & Legends
description: A challenging full-board covering the Old Testament, New Testament, classic rock and punk legends, home construction, parenting science, and gym and CrossFit knowledge.

questions.question: In Genesis, God commanded this patriarch to build an ark measuring exactly 300 cubits long, 50 cubits wide, and 30 cubits high — and to bring aboard two of every living creature to survive a flood that would cover the entire earth.

When the Pharaoh of Egypt was troubled by two dreams — seven fat cattle devoured by seven gaunt ones, and seven full ears of grain swallowed by seven withered ones — this favored son of Jacob gave the only interpretation that satisfied him: seven years of abundance followed by seven years of devastating famine.

The only woman named as a judge in the entire Book of Judges, this prophetess of Israel held court under a palm tree between Ramah and Bethel, summoned the military commander Barak to lead an army against the Canaanite general Sisera, and declared the honor of the final victory would go to a woman.

Serving as cupbearer to the Persian king Artaxerxes, this Jewish official obtained royal permission and funding to travel to Jerusalem — where he led the complete rebuilding of the city's ruined walls in just 52 days despite relentless opposition from the officials Sanballat and Tobiah.

At just 21 verses, this minor prophet's book — focused entirely on pronouncing divine judgment against the nation of Edom for its arrogance and for standing aside while Babylon sacked Jerusalem — holds the distinction of being the shortest book in the entire Old Testament.

Recorded in Matthew 6:9-13 and Luke 11:2-4, this prayer taught directly by Jesus begins with the address 'Our Father, who art in heaven' and includes petitions for daily bread, forgiveness of trespasses, and deliverance from evil — making it the most universally recited prayer in all of Christian history.

Because he was too short to see over the crowd lining the road, this wealthy chief tax collector of Jericho climbed a sycamore tree to catch a glimpse of Jesus — and was so transformed when Jesus declared he would stay at his house that he pledged to give half his possessions to the poor and repay anyone he had defrauded fourfold.

Traveling to Damascus with authorization to arrest early Christians, this Pharisee was struck to the ground by a blinding light, heard a voice asking 'Why do you persecute me?', was blind for three days before being healed by a disciple named Ananias, and went on to write at least 13 letters that form more of the New Testament than any other author.

In the second and third chapters of Revelation, the risen Christ dictates letters to this many specific churches in Asia Minor — including the famously 'lukewarm' church of Laodicea, which Christ threatens to 'spit out of my mouth' for being neither hot nor cold in their faith.

Both the Gospel of Luke and the Book of Acts are addressed to the same named individual — whose name translates from Greek as 'friend of God' or 'lover of God' — making him the only person in the New Testament to be the direct, named recipient of two entire books of Scripture.

All four members of this New York punk band adopted the same stage surname — inspired by the hotel check-in alias used by Paul McCartney — and their 1976 self-titled debut album, recorded in just seven days for $6,400, is widely ranked among the most influential and genre-defining rock recordings ever made.

When producers and the record label initially balked at releasing this nearly six-minute Queen track as a single, the band gave an advance copy to disc jockey Kenny Everett, who played it so relentlessly on air that overwhelming public demand made it impossible to hold back — and it became one of the best-selling singles in UK chart history.

Written by Creedence Clearwater Revival's John Fogerty in 1969 to protest the Vietnam-era practice of wealthy and well-connected young men evading military service, this furious rock anthem is considered one of the greatest anti-war songs in rock history — yet is frequently and ironically misused as a patriotic backdrop at political events and in war films.

When this CCR frontman released his 1985 solo comeback hit 'The Old Man Down the Road,' his former record label sued him — claiming the song plagiarized a track he himself had written decades earlier but had signed away — and he famously won the 1988 federal trial by picking up his guitar and performing both songs live for the jury.

Working with his father Harold using only hand tools, this Queen guitarist built his famous instrument from a Victorian fireplace mantel for the neck, oak salvaged from an old table for the body, and a bicycle saddlebag holder tipped with a plastic knitting needle as the tremolo arm — and has played it on virtually every Queen recording ever made.

Despite what their name implies, these ubiquitous pieces of dimensional lumber actually measure approximately 1.5 inches by 3.5 inches rather than the full dimensions their label suggests — and serve as the standard wall framing member in the overwhelming majority of residential wood-frame structures built in the United States.

Since the 1980s, this engineered wood panel — manufactured by compressing cross-oriented wood strands with resin and wax under high heat and pressure — has largely displaced plywood as the standard sheathing material for residential walls, floors, and roofs because it costs significantly less to produce.

In residential construction, this number printed on every roll of insulation and sheet of foam board measures a material's resistance to heat flow — with higher numbers meaning better thermal performance — and the International Residential Code mandates different minimums depending on climate zone and whether the application is an attic, wall, or floor.

Popular in American residential construction from roughly the 1830s through the mid-20th century, this framing method used long wall studs that ran continuously from the foundation sill plate all the way up to the roof plate in a single uninterrupted length — fundamentally different from today's platform framing, in which each floor acts as a separate structural level.

First published in the year 2000 by the International Code Council, this single comprehensive document unified the previously fragmented U.S. model building codes for one- and two-family dwellings into a single book covering structural, plumbing, mechanical, and electrical requirements — and has since been adopted in whole or part by most U.S. states.
questions.answer: What is the International Residential Code (IRC)?

questions.question: When Yale Law professor Amy Chua published her 2011 memoir describing how she raised two academically high-achieving daughters through relentless drilling, strict prohibitions on sleepovers and extracurricular choice, and zero tolerance for anything less than excellence, she earned this two-word nickname that sparked a global debate about cultural approaches to parenting.

In landmark research in the 1960s, this UC Berkeley developmental psychologist identified three primary parenting styles — authoritarian, permissive, and authoritative — and found through systematic observation that children raised by authoritative parents, who combined warmth with clear and consistent boundaries, showed the strongest academic performance and social competence.

Launched in 1994 by the National Institutes of Health, this public health campaign — which simply recommended placing infants on their backs to sleep rather than on their stomachs or sides — is credited with reducing the rate of sudden infant death syndrome in the United States by more than 50 percent in the decade that followed.
questions.answer: What is the 'Back to Sleep' campaign?

questions.question: In a series of landmark experiments at the University of Wisconsin in the late 1950s, this psychologist placed newborn rhesus monkeys with two artificial mothers — one bare wire that provided milk, one soft terry cloth that provided only contact — and discovered that the infants overwhelmingly clung to the cloth mother regardless of which one fed them, proving that physical comfort is the foundation of early attachment.

Developed by Mary Ainsworth in 1969, this laboratory procedure observed a toddler's behavior during a brief separation from and reunion with their primary caregiver — identifying three core attachment patterns (secure, anxious-avoidant, and anxious-ambivalent) — and became the cornerstone methodology of modern attachment theory research.

Named in honor of Navy SEAL Lieutenant Michael P. Murphy, who was killed in action in Afghanistan in 2005, this beloved CrossFit 'Hero WOD' consists of a one-mile run, 100 pull-ups, 200 push-ups, 300 air squats, and a final one-mile run — traditionally performed while wearing a 20-pound weight vest.

Published by Japanese sports scientist Izumi Tabata in a landmark 1996 paper, this high-intensity interval protocol — eight rounds of 20 seconds of all-out effort at 170 percent of VO2max followed by 10 seconds of complete rest — was the first protocol demonstrated to improve both aerobic capacity and anaerobic power simultaneously.

In this Olympic weightlifting movement — one of only two events contested at the Games alongside the clean and jerk — the barbell must travel from the floor to a fully locked-out overhead position in a single continuous, explosive movement, requiring the widest grip in the sport and extraordinary hip mobility and shoulder flexibility.

At this specific exercise intensity — typically around 80 to 85 percent of maximum heart rate for trained athletes — blood lactate begins to accumulate faster than working muscles can clear it, marking the critical boundary between sustainable aerobic effort and the zone where rapidly building acid fatigue limits high-intensity performance.

This physiological phenomenon — in which the body continues to consume oxygen at an elevated rate for hours after an intense workout as it replenishes depleted energy stores, restores oxygen levels in the blood, and repairs microtears in muscle tissue — is the scientific foundation behind fitness marketing claims about the 'afterburn effect' of HIIT and heavy resistance training.
questions.answer: What is EPOC (excess post-exercise oxygen consumption)?
